title: The Impossible Trilemma Behind Jensen Huang's Scandal
dek: The US wants to compete with China technologically and cannot cut welfare spending; history shows sound money gives way first—replicating the late-1960s trajectory before Bretton Woods collapsed.
why: Nvidia's stock crash, Jensen Huang's scandal, US-China decoupling, inflation, and gold—seemingly scattered news—are woven into one framework, suitable for anyone wanting to understand the macro backdrop of the AI bubble; specific stock prices will quickly become outdated.
who: Investors tracking the sustainability of AI capital expenditure, and macro researchers wanting to understand how US-China technology competition transmits to inflation and asset prices.

points.h: Chip Technology's Leaders Now Face Oppenheimer's Dilemma of Trust
points.body: Tianyang draws a direct parallel to Oppenheimer: a figure standing at the summit of critical technology, once a national hero, then scrutinized for state trustworthiness. While the specifics of any leak remain unclear, the argument is that chip technology now fuses nuclear-weapon potential with commercial opportunity, so when sovereignty enters the equation, pressure on such figures becomes inevitable.

points.h: Nations Now Prioritize Supply Chain Control Over Global Efficiency
points.body: Tianyang frames today's global trend as ‘sovereignty first’: countries have spotted hidden supply-chain vulnerabilities and are now systematically decoupling across chips, food, and energy. His example: China's moves starting with Syngenta to build seed autonomy eventually triggered US sanctions against ZTE and Huawei. Both sides are playing out self-reliance strategies on a decade-long timescale.

points.h: The Impossible Trilemma: Guns, Butter, and Sound Money Cannot Coexist
points.body: The framework: military and tech spending against China is fixed and off the table. Social media-driven polarization makes welfare cuts politically impossible. Historical pattern: when both are immovable, sound money yields first through continuous deficits. The present is on the same macro path as the 1960s before Bretton Woods fell.

points.h: Gold's Rise Today Echoes 1968, Signaling a Bretton Woods Crisis
points.body: Tianyang compares the gold surge since 2023 to 1968, on the eve of the London gold pool's collapse: the dollar's gold anchor was being eroded by persistent inflationary policy, France and others began dumping dollars and exiting the pool, until Nixon formally ended Bretton Woods in 1970-71. He sees today's gold anomaly as releasing the same warning signal early—though the full rupture may take longer.

points.h: To Make Financial Repression Work, Nations Must Control Capital Flight
points.body: An alternative to high debt is financial repression: maintain inflation at 4-5%, keep rates low to erode debt. But Tianyang argues this only works if capital cannot freely exit—so capital controls are quietly approaching. He points to Iran, China, and Russia imposing diesel-export bans, and Trump considering similar moves, as signals that ‘restricted flows’ are spreading from specific goods into a broader pattern.

points.h: Nvidia's Funding Demands Are Infinite Sprints, Not Sustainable Growth
points.body: Tianyang uses the metaphor of ‘a marathon made of nothing but 100-meter sprints’ for AI funding: labs need constant rapid financing to keep training momentum, with no time for normal due diligence—the source of circular financing and balance-sheet inversion. As Fed tightening and inflation pressure rise, each sprint faces stronger headwinds, and no one knows which sprint breaks the runner.

points.h: Government Funding of AI Will Determine Winners, Not Market Competition
points.body: Tianyang concedes private capital can't easily monetize AI alone, but if the logic is ‘nukes have no economic return yet deserve funding,’ governments will eventually join—with conditions. They'll mandate domestic-supplier preferences, trapping capital at home to inflate local assets while excluding foreign suppliers. AI's winners will be decided by ‘national team’ ranking, not market efficiency.

points.h: Iran Conflict Could Trigger the Impossible Trilemma Decision
points.body: Tianyang sees the Iran conflict as a trigger for the trilemma choice, since war, once started, is hard to stop and keeps squeezing sovereign resources. He sees three paths forward: a Ross Perot-style populist push to cut spending, a Peronist-style extreme turn, or a public backlash against data centers and AI expansion—treated as a real outcome, not mere speculation.

terms.def: Military spending, welfare, and sound money are mutually exclusive; one must be sacrificed.
Using suppressed interest rates and mild inflation to gradually reduce government debt burden.
A 1960s multinational effort to maintain the gold standard, whose breakdown in 1968 signaled Bretton Woods' coming collapse.
Capital flowing in circles through related companies (chipmakers, cloud providers, AI labs) that invest in and serve each other.

quotes.text: So as I started saying a bit earlier, it's really about sovereignty's idea of being able to say no. So you don't want to feel dependent.
So the trinity is this idea because you have this rivalry against foreign powers, you're spending on guns and your mobilization, that's locked in. It's non-negotiable.
Then the tension becomes, if you're committed to your guns spending and you're committed to your butter spending, then history shows that typically the leg that gives way is sound money.

So in my mind, this is almost like you're running a marathon because just the sheer amount of financing we need to raise in the next few years. But because of all these pressures, every marginal fundraise is like a sprint.
The government might mandate everything you buy comes from the US locally. So then you inject a lot of stimulus into the system. It's all kept here.
But if you bought the fifth... frontier AI lab that doesn't have enough compute. I don't think that's a good investment, right?
It's a Sisyphean marathon. That never ends.
